title: A client-owned account is operated with one access stack
description:
```gherkin
Feature: A client grants access with one stack

  Scenario: The client launches one stack
    Given a client with their own AWS account
    When they launch the access stack from a link, giving a deployment name
    Then it creates one role our pipeline can assume, requiring an external id, with the same permission ceiling as the seeded roles
    And the client can delete the stack to revoke all access

  Scenario: Our pipeline does the rest
    Given the access stack exists
    When we merge a change in the operating repository
    Then the pipeline seeds the baseline and deploys the stacks in the client's account
    And the client's data and keys stay in the client's account
```

comments.author: home
comments.text:
# Design: a client-owned account is operated with one access stack (managed offer)

The client launches ONE CloudFormation stack that grants us access. Our pipeline then seeds the account baseline (docs/account-pipeline.md) and deploys everything else. Nobody creates anything by hand, in their account or ours. Design only; nothing is built.

## 1. The access stack (`infra/account/access.yaml`, to be written)
| Resource | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `papyrus-access-operate` role | Trusted only by our broker role. Requires `sts:ExternalId`, `sts:SourceIdentity` and session tags `client` and `run`. One-hour sessions (the limit for chained roles). |
| `papyrus-access-read` role | View-only role for our agents, with explicit denies on data reads: `s3:GetObject`, DynamoDB item reads, `ssm:GetParameter*` with decryption, `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`, `kms:Decrypt`. |
| Permission boundary policy | The ceiling. Allows the services Papyrus uses (Amplify, AppSync, Lambda, DynamoDB, S3, Cognito, CloudFront, Route 53, ACM, SES, SSM, Budgets, CloudFormation). Denies IAM users and access keys, leaving or changing an organization, stopping CloudTrail or Config, and changing or deleting the access stack. |
| Role-creation rule | The operate role may create roles only with the same boundary (`iam:PermissionsBoundary` condition), which also caps the app shell's Amplify service role (AdministratorAccess today). |
| Optional baseline seed | A parameter creates the GitHub OIDC provider; otherwise our pipeline applies the unchanged `baseline.yaml` through the operate role. |
Parameters: `DeploymentName` (the prefix), `ExternalId`, `AccessPrincipalArn`. Our account id appears in the template; the client's never leaves their account.

## 2. How the client launches it
- A CloudFormation quick-create link (`templateURL`, `stackName`, `param_*`). The template must be in S3, so a release workflow publishes it from a tag to a bucket in our operations account (itself defined in Git; Block Public Access relaxed for the `access/*` prefix only). Public read is fine: the template holds no secret, and the client's security team can read it before launching.
- Immutable versioned paths (`access/1.4.0/access.yaml`), S3 Versioning on, SHA-256 and a GitHub build attestation published with each release.
- A change to our reach arrives only when the client updates the stack to a newer path: that update is the one place the client approves our ceiling.
- To verify before the first client: that quick-create accepts a template bucket in a different region.

## 3. How our pipeline assumes the role
- GitHub OIDC signs in to a per-client `broker` role in our operations account; it has `sts:AssumeRole` on that client's operate role and nothing else. Each call sets SourceIdentity `<repo>@<run id>` and the session tags, which appear in the client's CloudTrail.
- ExternalId: random, 32+ characters, unique per client, generated by us. It prevents the confused-deputy problem across clients; it is kept in an SSM SecureString in the operations account and never printed. A person puts it there once (CloudFormation cannot create a SecureString).
- After the seed, a public-repo deployment goes straight through the baseline's OIDC roles (no chain, no ExternalId); the operate role is then for baseline changes and break-glass.

## 4. Who does what
Client: their AWS account, the access stack, registrar delegation, secret values. Our pipeline: the baseline, account stacks (DNS, budget, certificate, SES, placeholder) and Papyrus version bumps. Our agents: read-only through the read role.

## 5. Revoke, and what we can see
- Revoking = deleting the access stack; both roles disappear at once and the pipeline fails closed. The baseline stack and OIDC roles are separate, so offboarding also deletes the baseline stack (we ship a one-line command). Pipeline-made zones and budgets keep `DeletionPolicy: Retain`.
- We can see resource metadata, stack events, CloudTrail and cost. By default we cannot read object contents, table items, secret values or decrypted parameters.
- Honest limit: the operate role can deploy code, and code can read data. The controls are the boundary, the client's CloudTrail, SourceIdentity tags and the contract. We must not claim we cannot read data.

## 6. Per-client repository and pipeline
Each client gets `<org>/<client>-papyrus` with `infra/stacks.json`, `expected-nameservers.json`, `allowed-changes.json`, a version pin and the caller workflow.
| | Public repo | Private repo |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CI/CD | GitHub Actions and OIDC with the reusable `account-stacks.yml` | CodePipeline V2 and CodeBuild running `stack_deploy.py` |
| Cost | Free | CodeBuild about a cent or two a deploy; Actions minutes beyond quota billed (verify prices) |
| Exposure | Client name and domain visible; logs public | Nothing visible |
Recommendation: private by default, pipeline in our operations account (we bear the small cost; the client's account stays free of our CI). The CodeBuild variant is not built. Its GitHub connection (CodeConnections) needs a one-time browser authorization by a person. Option to check: CodeBuild-hosted GitHub Actions runners to reuse the workflow files.

## 7. Updates, offboarding, cost
Updates: a bot PR changes the pinned Papyrus tag; merging deploys; the client can hold a version back by closing the PR. Handover: repoint `GithubRepository` to the client's repo, then the client deletes the access stack. Cost to us: cents per client per month. Cost to the client: their own AWS usage (a hosted zone is about 0.50 USD a month) plus our fee.

## 8. Person-only steps
Client creates the account and root MFA; client launches the stack; we put the ExternalId in SSM; client delegates the registrar name servers; client creates the Google OAuth client; someone puts secret values in place; one-time GitHub connection for private repos; SES production access and the budget alert address in SSM.

## 9. Not built
`access.yaml`; the broker roles; the CodeBuild variant; the release workflow that publishes to S3; and a test of the boundary against the real app-shell roles (the biggest unknown).
